plan: SAT R&W batch 57: 8 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000512..000519, written to test whether denser source texts (academic argument, a dense critical passage, a public-domain Dickinson poem, a subtle cross-text study) raise blind-rated difficulty where distractor design alone did not. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Cathedrals by committee
passages.text: In arguing that the medieval cathedral was less the monument to a single vision than an accretion of compromises among bishops, guilds, and successive master builders, the historian does not ______ the achievement of those who built it; rather, she relocates it, crediting collective negotiation with what earlier accounts had ascribed to individual genius.

passages.title: Inventors and cities
passages.text: Economists have long observed that cities produce more patents per resident than rural areas do, and many have attributed the difference to the density of face-to-face contact among inventors. Yet the pattern admits another explanation: unusually inventive people may simply move to cities, bringing their productivity with them. To separate these possibilities, researchers followed individual inventors who relocated and found that the same people patented more after moving into larger clusters of inventors in their field, a result that the sorting explanation alone cannot accommodate.

passages.title: Translating what is left open
passages.text: Translators of classical Chinese poetry face a peculiar difficulty. The originals often leave grammatical subject, tense, and number unstated, so that a line may describe one traveler or many, an event now or long past. English, which demands such choices, forces the translator to settle what the poem leaves open. Some translators accept this as an unavoidable loss; others have experimented with fragmentary English that preserves the openness at the cost of fluency. Neither approach, the critic argues, escapes the problem, for one sacrifices the poem's ambiguity and the other its ease, which is no less a part of its meaning.

passages.title: Words for blue
passages.text:
Text 1
Some scholars have argued that the language a person speaks determines what that person can perceive: if a language lacks separate words for two colors, its speakers cannot truly see them as different.

Text 2
Russian has two basic words for blue: goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker ones. In one experiment, Russian speakers were faster than English speakers at telling apart two blues that fell on opposite sides of that boundary. But the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they performed a verbal task, such as silently repeating a string of digits, at the same time, while a nonverbal task did not remove it. Language, the researchers concluded, can influence perception, but through the words people use in the moment.

passages.title: Hope
passages.text:
The following text is from Emily Dickinson's poem "'Hope' is the thing with feathers," written around 1861.
"Hope" is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -
And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -
I've heard it in the chillest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of me.

passages.title: E-book loans
passages.text:
A county library system reported the number of e-books it loaned each year.
2017: 40,000
2018: 44,000
2019: 48,000
2020: 75,000
2021: 82,000
A researcher claims that the jump in e-book loans after 2019 was not simply a continuation of the system's earlier trend.

passages.title: Whale songs
passages.text: Having analyzed thousands of hours of underwater recordings collected over a decade, ______

passages.title: Bridge from a window
passages.text: By the time the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its chief engineer, Washington Roebling, ______ construction for more than a decade from a room overlooking the East River, having been disabled by decompression sickness he developed while working in the bridge's underwater foundations.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.explanation: "Rather, she relocates it" corrects a possible misreading: that by denying a single vision she lessens the builders' achievement. She does not "diminish" it; she assigns it to collective negotiation.

B.rationale: She does recognize the achievement, so saying she does not acknowledge it contradicts "crediting collective negotiation."

C.rationale: Her argument is itself an investigation of how the cathedrals were made, so denying that she investigates makes no sense.

D.rationale: Earlier accounts may have romanticized individual genius, but "rather, she relocates it" answers a charge of reducing the achievement, not of idealizing it.

hints: What does "rather, she relocates it" correct?
candidates.remember: After "not X; rather Y," X is what a reader might wrongly assume.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a finding, identifies a flaw in the research behind it, and concludes that the finding is unreliable.
choices.B: It describes a theory about inventors, offers evidence supporting it, and then shows that the evidence is flawed.
choices.C: It notes a pattern, raises an alternative to a common explanation of it, and describes a study that distinguishes the two.
choices.D: It compares two explanations for a pattern and argues that the evidence supports each of them equally well.

candidates.evidence: a result that the sorting explanation alone cannot accommodate
candidates.explanation: The text reports more patents in cities, offers sorting as an alternative to the face-to-face explanation, and describes a study of relocating inventors that tells the explanations apart.

A.rationale: The pattern itself is not called unreliable; the text questions only its explanation.

B.rationale: The study at the end supports the density explanation rather than exposing a flaw in evidence.

D.rationale: The final study favors one explanation, since sorting alone cannot account for its result.

hints: What job does each sentence do?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence, then match the sequence.

candidates.remember: Describe the job of each part, not its topic.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A critic holds that fragmentary English versions are more faithful to classical Chinese poems than fluent ones.
choices.B: A critic holds that English versions of classical Chinese poems must lose something, whether openness or ease.
choices.C: A critic holds that the ambiguity of classical Chinese poems was not intended by the poets who wrote them.
choices.D: A critic holds that classical Chinese poetry cannot be translated into English and should be read in the original.

candidates.evidence: Neither approach, the critic argues, escapes the problem
candidates.explanation: The text explains why English forces choices the originals leave open and concludes with the critic's view that both strategies lose something: ambiguity or ease.

A.rationale: The critic says fragmentary versions sacrifice ease, which is also part of the meaning, so neither approach is favored.

C.rationale: The text says nothing about what the poets intended.

D.rationale: The critic identifies an unavoidable loss, not impossibility, and makes no recommendation about reading the originals.

hints: What does the critic conclude about both approaches?
candidates.remember: The main idea often comes in a text's final judgment.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?

choices.A: They would agree, since Russian speakers saw differences between blues that English speakers could not see.
choices.B: They would reject any role for language in perception, since the Russian speakers' advantage could be removed.
choices.C: They would say that the claim is supported for color but should be tested for other kinds of perception.
choices.D: They would say that language can speed some perceptual judgments but does not fix what speakers are able to see.

candidates.evidence: through the words people use in the moment
candidates.explanation: Text 2 shows a real but limited effect: Russian speakers were faster, but only when verbal processing was available. That supports influence, not the determination Text 1 claims.

A.rationale: English speakers could still tell the blues apart; they were only slower.

B.rationale: The researchers conclude that language can influence perception, though not in the way Text 1 claims.

C.rationale: The results contradict the strong claim even for color, because the effect depends on in-the-moment verbal processing.

hints: Does Text 2 show that language determines perception, or something weaker?

strategy.explanation: Compare the strength of each text's claim.

candidates.remember: Watch for responses that accept a weaker version of a claim.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (illustrate a claim)
candidates.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim that hope persists through the harshest conditions while demanding nothing of the speaker?

choices.A: "And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -"
choices.B: "I've heard it in the chillest land - / And on the strangest Sea -"
choices.C: "Yet - never - in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of me."
choices.D: "That could abash the little Bird / That kept so many warm -"

candidates.evidence: It asked a crumb - of me.
candidates.explanation: "In Extremity" names the harshest conditions, and "never ... asked a crumb" shows that hope demands nothing, so these lines support both parts of the claim.

A.rationale: This shows that hope persists, but not in harsh conditions and not that it asks nothing of the speaker.

B.rationale: This places hope in harsh conditions but says nothing about what hope asks of the speaker.

D.rationale: This suggests hope comforts many people, but not that it asks nothing in return.

hints: Which lines show both extreme conditions and asking nothing?

strategy.explanation: Check each quotation for both halves of the claim.

candidates.remember: The quotation must support every part of the claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the researcher's claim?

choices.A: Loans grew by about 4,000 each year from 2017 to 2019 but by 27,000 from 2019 to 2020.
choices.B: Loans in 2021 were more than twice as high as loans in 2017.
choices.C: Loans increased in every year from 2017 through 2021.
choices.D: Loans grew by 7,000 from 2020 to 2021, compared with 4,000 from 2018 to 2019.

candidates.evidence: was not simply a continuation of the system's earlier trend
candidates.explanation: To show a break from the trend, compare the earlier yearly growth (about 4,000) with the growth after 2019 (27,000). Only choice A makes that comparison.

B.rationale: This is true, but steady growth over four years could also double loans, so it does not separate the jump from the trend.

C.rationale: Steady yearly increases are what an ongoing trend would produce, so this does not support the claim.

D.rationale: This compares two modest increases and leaves out the large jump from 2019 to 2020.

hints: What would a continued trend have predicted for 2020?

strategy.explanation: Compute the earlier yearly change, then compare.

candidates.remember: To show a break in a trend, compare the change with the earlier rate.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the conclusion of the team was that humpback whale songs change gradually over a breeding season.
choices.B: the team concluded that humpback whale songs change gradually over a breeding season.
choices.C: humpback whale songs were found by the team to change gradually over a breeding season.
choices.D: it was concluded by the team that humpback whale songs change gradually over a breeding season.

candidates.evidence: Having analyzed thousands of hours of underwater recordings
candidates.explanation: The people who analyzed the recordings are the team, so "the team" must come right after the opening phrase.

A.rationale: The opening phrase would describe "the conclusion," which cannot analyze recordings.

C.rationale: The opening phrase would describe the songs, which did not analyze anything.

D.rationale: The opening phrase would describe "it," not the team that did the analysis.

strategy.explanation: Put the doer right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier describes the noun that follows it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: By the time the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883
candidates.explanation: "By the time" a past event happened, an action that had continued for a stretch of time before it takes the past perfect progressive: "had been directing."

A.rationale: The present tense does not fit an action completed before the 1883 opening.

B.rationale: The present perfect connects to the present, not to a time before a past event.

C.rationale: The past progressive does not show an action continuing up to an earlier past time, which "by the time" and "for more than a decade" require.

hints: What does "by the time" plus a past event require?

strategy.explanation: Find the time words that set the tense.

candidates.remember: Use the past perfect for actions before another past event.
